pos: n. (Olaudah Equiano, also called Gustavus Vassa, c. 1745–1797, freed slave, evangelical convert, and author of the Interesting Narrative of 1789)
etymology: Igbo Olaudah, explained by Equiano as one favoured, having a loud voice; Equiano, his family name.
biblical_def: Olaudah Equiano wrote that he was born in the Igbo country of West Africa, kidnapped as a child, and carried through the Middle Passage to the West Indies and Virginia. He was bought by a British naval officer, Michael Pascal, who renamed him Gustavus Vassa and took him to sea through the Seven Years' War; later sold to Robert King, a Quaker merchant of Montserrat, he traded on his own account and in 1766 bought his freedom for forty pounds. In 1774, after years of religious searching, he was converted aboard ship while reading the Acts of the Apostles, finding peace in the truth that “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12). He joined the abolition movement in London, brought the Zong massacre to Granville Sharp's attention in 1783, served briefly as commissary for the Sierra Leone resettlement scheme until he was dismissed for exposing its mismanagement, and in 1789 published The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, which went through nine editions in his lifetime and made the slave trade a thing Englishmen could not pretend not to see. The abolitionists who printed his book knew the law of Moses against his captors, that “he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) shall surely be put to death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a slave as a person wholly subject to the will of another, and a narrative as a relation of particulars.
webster_full: SLAVE, n. A person who is wholly subject to the will of another; one who has no will of his own, but whose person and services are wholly under the control of another.
MAN'STEALER, n. One who steals and sells men.
NAR'RATIVE, n. The recital of a story, or a continued account of the particulars of an event or transaction.
scriptures: And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Phm 1:16
Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?
corruption_summary: A freed slave converted by the Acts of the Apostles, whose book indicted the trade in men.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the Atlantic slave trade as manstealing, which the law of God punishes with death and the apostle lists among the sins “contrary to sound doctrine” (1Ti 1:10). Equiano's testimony is that the trade was defended by baptized men who knew their Bibles. Paul's sermon at Athens had already answered the theory of race that propped it up: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26).

The modern corruption runs the other way: to treat Equiano only as a voice of protest and to leave out the faith that formed him. His Narrative is a conversion narrative before it is anything else, and the freedom he valued most was the one Paul describes to Philemon, “a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16) in the Lord. An account of him that keeps the politics and drops the gospel has not read his book.
roots_summary: Hebrew ganab (H1589), to steal; makar (H4376), to sell; Greek soteria (G4991), salvation.
usage: “none other name under heaven” (Act 4:12) — the verse of his conversion.
“of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26) — the answer to race slavery.
“Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16) — the freedom of the gospel.

pos: n. (the chartered company founded in 1791 by Henry Thornton and the Clapham abolitionists to settle freed slaves in West Africa)
etymology: Portuguese Serra Leoa, lion mountain; Latin companio, one who shares bread.
biblical_def: The Sierra Leone Company was incorporated by Act of Parliament in 1791 to take over a failing settlement of the poor black population of London, begun in 1787 at the instigation of Granville Sharp. Its chairman was the banker Henry Thornton, and its directors included William Wilberforce, Thomas Clarkson, and Sharp. The directors meant the colony to prove that legitimate trade with Africa could replace the trade in men, and that Africans governing themselves under Christian law could prosper. In January 1792 John Clarkson, Thomas's brother, brought nearly twelve hundred black Loyalists from Nova Scotia, men and women who had escaped slavery by fighting for Britain in the American war, and they founded Freetown. The colony suffered fever, a French naval attack in 1794, quarrels over land and taxation, and a settler rebellion in 1800; Zachary Macaulay governed it through its hardest years. In 1808 the bankrupt company surrendered it to the Crown, and Freetown became the base from which the Royal Navy landed tens of thousands of Africans freed from captured slave ships, and from which the Church Missionary Society reached West Africa. Its founders acted on the prophet's fast: “to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke” (Isa 58:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a company of people transplanted to a remote country, and a company as an association of persons for carrying on a commercial undertaking.
webster_full: COL'ONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country to cultivate and inhabit it.
COM'PANY, n. A number of persons united for the same purpose, or in a joint concern; as a company of merchants.
CHAR'TER, n. An instrument executed in due form, given as evidence of a grant of privileges.
scriptures: Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
Pro 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
Psa 68:6
God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: A Clapham experiment in freedom, commerce, and Christian settlement on the coast of West Africa.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Recent accounts often reduce the Sierra Leone scheme to paternalism or to the first chapter of colonial rule. The honest record contains both real paternalism and real mercy. The directors were often high-handed with settlers who had won their own freedom and wanted a voice in their own government, and the settlers' grievances were just. But the men who chartered the company spent their own fortunes on it, and it is the reason Freetown exists.

The principle to recover is the duty of Pro 31:8, “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8), joined to the humility to learn from those one means to help. The God who “bringeth out those which are bound with chains” (Psa 68:6) does not need men to be masters of the freed.
roots_summary: Hebrew ratsats (H7533), to oppress, crush; chophshi (H2670), free; motah (H4133), yoke.
usage: “let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6) — the purpose of the charter.
“Open thy mouth for the dumb” (Pro 31:8) — Clapham's commission.
“neither bond nor free” (Gal 3:28) — one people in Christ.

pos: n. (the society founded by William Wilberforce in 1787 to enforce the royal proclamation against vice and immorality)
biblical_def: The Proclamation Society was Wilberforce's second great cause. In the same year that he wrote in his journal that God had set before him two great objects, the suppression of the slave trade and the reformation of manners, he persuaded the Archbishop of Canterbury and others to obtain from George III a royal Proclamation for the Encouragement of Piety and Virtue, and for the Preventing and Punishing of Vice, Profaneness, and Immorality, issued on 1 June 1787. Wilberforce then organized a society of bishops, peers, and magistrates to see that the proclamation was enforced, urging local justices to act against drunkenness, Sabbath-breaking, blasphemy, gambling houses, and the sale of obscene publications. In 1797 the society brought the prosecution of Thomas Williams for publishing Thomas Paine's Age of Reason. In 1802 its work passed to the more vigorous Society for the Suppression of Vice. Critics mocked it as a scheme to police the pleasures of the poor while sparing the rich; Wilberforce's answer was that the example must begin at the top, and that a nation's laws teach as well as restrain. His conviction was the proverb's: “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a proclamation as an official public notice given by the supreme authority, and vice as any voluntary action contrary to the moral law.
webster_full: PROCLAMA'TION, n. Official notice given to the public; an official public notice given by the supreme executive of a kingdom or state.
VICE, n. In ethics, any voluntary action or course of conduct which deviates from the rules of moral rectitude, or from the plain rules of propriety.
PROFANE'NESS, n. Irreverence of sacred things; particularly, the use of language which implies irreverence towards God.
scriptures: Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
Rom 13:3
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
Eph 5:11
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
corruption_summary: Wilberforce's campaign for the reformation of manners under royal proclamation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern readers find the Proclamation Society embarrassing, a puritanical intrusion that sits awkwardly beside the abolition campaign. Wilberforce saw no such division. The magistrate who protects the slave and the magistrate who restrains public vice are the same minister of God, of whom Paul says “rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3).

The honest caveat is the critics' own: law that falls hardest on the poor while the fashionable sin in comfort is not righteousness but respectability. The principle to recover is that the church's first weapon against vice is not the constable but reproof and example: “have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11).
roots_summary: Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666), righteousness; chesed (H2617), reproach; Greek elegcho (G1651), to reprove.
roots_lines: Hebrew chesed (H2617) — here a reproach, shame; Proverbs 14:34.
usage: “sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34) — the case for reformation of manners.
“not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3) — the magistrate's office.
“but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11) — the church's part.

pos: n. (Edward Bickersteth, 1786–1850, evangelical clergyman, secretary of the Church Missionary Society, and a founder of the Evangelical Alliance)
etymology: Old English Eadweard, rich guardian; Bickersteth, a Lancashire place-name.
biblical_def: Edward Bickersteth was a Norwich solicitor who left the law for the ministry of the Church of England and became, in 1816, a secretary of the Church Missionary Society. He travelled to Sierra Leone to inspect its missions, built up its home organization, and trained its missionaries. From 1830 until his death he was rector of Watton in Hertfordshire, where he preached, wrote, and kept open house for evangelical clergy. His books — A Scripture Help, A Treatise on Prayer, The Christian Student, and others — sold in great numbers and shaped the devotional life of early Victorian evangelicals. In later life he became an earnest premillennialist of the historicist school, reading the prophecies of Daniel and Revelation as fulfilled in the papacy and looking for the Lord's near return; he was a determined opponent of the Oxford Movement, whose Romeward course he thought the great danger of the church. In 1846 he helped found the Evangelical Alliance, an attempt to unite Protestants of many denominations on a shared evangelical confession. He held “a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19), and prayed with the end of the Bible, “Even so, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion, and prophecy as a foretelling of future events.
webster_full: MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion. Christian missionaries are called missionaries of the cross.
PROPH'ECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
AL'LIANCE, n. The relation or union between persons by agreement or treaty.
scriptures: We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: A CMS secretary and prophetic writer who answered Tractarianism and helped found the Evangelical Alliance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bickersteth's life gathers the strengths of early Victorian evangelicalism: missionary zeal, devotional seriousness, plain preaching, and the conviction that Rome's errors were errors. His opposition to Tractarianism was clear-eyed; the movement he resisted did end, for many of its leaders, in Rome. He was ready, as Peter commands, “to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15).

The honest caveat is the Evangelical Alliance itself, which sought unity on a minimal common creed. The principle to recover is that the unity of Eph 4:3, “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3), is a unity in the whole faith confessed, and that alliances built on the smallest agreement tend to make the smallest agreement the measure of orthodoxy.
roots_lines: Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to endeavour, be diligent; Ephesians 4:3.
usage: “a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19) — his prophetic studies.
“Even so, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20) — the hope of Watton rectory.
“a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15) — his answer to Oxford.

pos: n. (Hugh McNeile, 1795–1879, Irish-born evangelical preacher of Liverpool, anti-Tractarian controversialist, and Dean of Ripon)
etymology: Old French Hue, from Germanic hugi, mind; Irish Mac Neill, son of Niall.
biblical_def: Hugh McNeile was born in County Antrim, trained for the bar, and was ordained in the Church of England. As rector of Albury in Surrey from 1822 he was drawn into the circle of the banker Henry Drummond and took part in the Albury conferences on unfulfilled prophecy, though he drew back when Edward Irving's followers turned to tongues and new apostles. In 1834 he went to Liverpool, first to St Jude's and later to St Paul's, Prince's Park, and for over thirty years he was the most powerful Protestant preacher in the north of England. Liverpool was then filling with Irish Catholic immigrants and becoming the scene of sharp religious conflict, and McNeile preached and lectured unsparingly against the doctrines of Rome and against the Tractarian movement in the Church of England, which he regarded as Rome's advance guard. He defended the Protestant constitution, opposed the state endowment of the Catholic seminary at Maynooth, and drew huge congregations. In 1868 he was made Dean of Ripon. His texts were the apostle's warning, “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8), and the call of Rev 18:4, “Come out of her, my people” (Rev 18:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines popery as the religion of the Roman Catholic Church, comprehending doctrines and practices.
webster_full: PO'PERY, n. The religion of the church of Rome, comprehending doctrines and practices.
CONTROVER'SIALIST, n. One who carries on a controversy; a disputant.
DEAN, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary in cathedral and collegiate churches, and the head of the chapter.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Rev 18:4
And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.
Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: A Liverpool preacher who named Rome's errors and Tractarianism's drift in the plainest terms.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the Tractarian movement as the corruption McNeile said it was: a recovery within the Church of England of sacramental regeneration, priestly absolution, the sacrifice of the mass, and the honour of the saints, which ended for Newman, Manning, and many others in Rome itself. The papal claim it led toward is the one 2Th 2:4 describes, he “Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God” (2Th 2:4), as the Reformers and the Westminster divines read it.

The honest caveat is the setting. In a city torn by sectarian riot, preaching that named Rome's doctrines could be heard as hostility to Irish Catholic neighbours, and McNeile did not always guard the distinction. The principle to recover is the apostle's: test the spirits, “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1), and love the men while refusing the system.
roots_summary: Greek anathema (G331), accursed; huperairomai (G5229), to exalt oneself; dokimazo (G1381), to try.
roots_lines: Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to preach the gospel; Galatians 1:8.
Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8.
Greek sugkoinoneo (G4790) — to be partaker with; Revelation 18:4.
Greek huperairomai (G5229) — to exalt oneself above; 2 Thessalonians 2:4.
usage: “preach any other gospel” (Gal 1:8) — his charge against Tractarianism.
“Come out of her, my people” (Rev 18:4) — the Protestant appeal.
“try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1) — controversy as duty.

pos: n. (Francis Close, 1797–1882, evangelical incumbent of Cheltenham for thirty years, educational founder, and Dean of Carlisle)
biblical_def: Francis Close was a Cambridge evangelical of Charles Simeon's school who in 1826 became perpetual curate of the parish church of Cheltenham, then a fashionable spa town of racecourses, theatres, and assembly rooms. He held the charge until 1856 and so dominated the town's religious and civic life that his enemies called him the Pope of Cheltenham. He built new churches and schools, founded Cheltenham College in 1841 and a training college for teachers in 1847 to supply Christian schoolmasters, and campaigned against the races, the theatre, and the desecration of the Lord's Day with a persistence that won as many enemies as admirers. He was an outspoken opponent of the Tractarians, preaching and publishing against what he called the Romanizing of the Church of England, and an advocate of the Protestant character of the Prayer Book and the Articles. In 1856 he was made Dean of Carlisle, where he served for twenty-five years and in later life became a strong advocate of total abstinence. His Sabbatarianism rested on the fourth commandment, “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8), and on Isaiah's promise to those who “call the sabbath a delight” (Isa 58:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Sabbatarian as one who observes the sabbath strictly, and a curate as a clergyman who has the care of souls.
webster_full: SABBATA'RIAN, n. One who observes the seventh day of the week as the sabbath; also, one who is strict in observing the sabbath.
CU'RATE, n. One who is employed to perform divine service in the place of the incumbent; one who has the cure of souls.
ABSTI'NENCE, n. The act or practice of voluntarily refraining from the use of any thing within our power.
scriptures: Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:
Mar 2:27
And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath:
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: An evangelical incumbent who made a spa town keep the Lord's Day and built schools to teach its children.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Close is usually remembered as a caricature, the clergyman who closed the theatres. The caricature omits the schools, the churches, the training college, and thirty years of preaching. His Sabbatarianism was not a private scruple but the fourth commandment, and the church that has abandoned the Lord's Day has not grown freer but poorer.

The honest caveat is that zeal for the Sabbath can forget Christ's own word, “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath” (Mar 2:27), and become a regime rather than a delight. The principle to recover is Isaiah's: the day is kept best by those who find in it “the holy of the LORD, honourable” (Isa 58:13), and who teach their children to love it as Close's schools tried to teach the children of Cheltenham.
roots_lines: Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to sanctify, keep holy; Exodus 20:8.
usage: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8) — the commandment he preached.
“call the sabbath a delight” (Isa 58:13) — the spirit of true observance.
“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — the Cheltenham schools.

pos: n. (the legal controversy of 1847–1850 over the Bishop of Exeter's refusal to institute George Gorham, who denied unconditional baptismal regeneration)
etymology: Gorham, an English surname from a place-name; Latin casus, a falling, an event.
biblical_def: The Gorham Case arose when George Cornelius Gorham, an evangelical clergyman, was presented in 1847 to the living of Brampford Speke in the diocese of Exeter. Henry Phillpotts, the High Church bishop, examined him for some fifty hours on the doctrine of baptism and refused to institute him because Gorham would not affirm that every infant is regenerated in the act of baptism; Gorham held that regeneration is given only to worthy recipients, and that in infants it depends on God's prevenient grace, not on the rite. The Court of Arches upheld the bishop in 1849. In March 1850 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, a lay court on which the archbishops sat only as advisers, reversed the decision, ruling that Gorham's view was not contrary to the formularies of the Church of England. Evangelicals rejoiced; High Churchmen were appalled that a secular court had decided a question of doctrine, and in the years that followed Henry Manning, Robert Wilberforce, and others went over to Rome. The case turned on Tit 3:5, where Paul speaks of “the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost” (Tit 3:5), and on what the washing is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines regeneration as new birth by the grace of God, and institution as the investiture of a clerk with the spiritual part of a benefice.
webster_full: REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God and his law are subdued.
INSTITU'TION, n. In the canon law, the investiture of a clerk with a spiritual benefice.
BAP'TISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony.
scriptures: Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Joh 3:5
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: A right verdict on baptismal regeneration reached by the wrong court.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the bishop's position, that regeneration is bestowed in and by the act of baptism upon every infant, as corruption of the sacrament. Peter says plainly that baptism saves “not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God” (1Pe 3:21), and the Reformed confessions deny that grace and salvation are so inseparably annexed to the ordinance that all who are baptized are undoubtedly regenerated.

The second corruption is the one the Tractarians saw and the evangelicals were too relieved to notice: a church whose doctrine is finally settled by a committee of lawyers appointed by the crown has an Erastian constitution. The principle to recover is that both Gorham and his bishop should have been judged by a church court bound by Scripture. A right answer from the wrong authority does not secure the next answer.
roots_lines: Greek suntheptomai (G4916) — to be buried with; Romans 6:4.
usage: “the washing of regeneration” (Tit 3:5) — the disputed text.
“the answer of a good conscience toward God” (1Pe 3:21) — what baptism is not, and is.
“born of water and of the Spirit” (Joh 3:5) — the sign and the thing signified.

pos: n. (William Stoughton, 1631–1701, lieutenant governor of Massachusetts and chief judge of the Salem witchcraft court of 1692)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, will and helmet; English Stoughton, a place-name, stone farmstead.
biblical_def: William Stoughton was a Harvard graduate and preacher who never took a pastorate and instead became one of the leading magistrates of Massachusetts. In 1668 he preached the colony's election sermon, New-Englands True Interest, with its famous line that God had sifted a whole nation that He might send choice grain over into the wilderness. In 1692, as lieutenant governor, he was appointed chief judge of the special Court of Oyer and Terminer convened at Salem to try the accused in the witchcraft outbreak. Under his direction the court admitted spectral evidence, the testimony of afflicted persons that the spectre or shape of the accused had tormented them, and Stoughton held that the devil could not take the shape of an innocent person. Nineteen people were hanged and one pressed to death before Governor Phips dissolved the court in October. When in early 1693 Governor Phips reprieved condemned prisoners whose death warrants Stoughton had signed, Stoughton left the bench in anger. Unlike his fellow judge Samuel Sewall, who stood in his church in 1697 and publicly confessed his guilt, Stoughton never repented. The court he led broke the law of witnesses: “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deu 19:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines witchcraft as the practices of witches, and evidence as that which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth.
webster_full: WITCH'CRAFT, n. The practices of witches; sorcery; enchantments; intercourse with the devil.
EV'IDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our perceptions by the senses, or from the testimony of others.
MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
scriptures: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
corruption_summary: The judge of Salem who hanged the innocent on spectral evidence and never repented.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names Stoughton's court as a corruption of justice, and does so on Puritan grounds. The law of God requires evidence that two or three witnesses can establish, and spectral evidence is no evidence at all: it is the unverifiable report of a vision, and Scripture warns that such visions must be tested, “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits” (1Jn 4:1). Increase Mather's Cases of Conscience made the point in 1692: better that ten suspected witches escape than one innocent person be condemned.

The modern use of Salem to discredit the Puritans and the Bible alike gets the lesson backward. The executions were stopped by Puritan ministers applying Scripture's rules of evidence, and the most honourable act of the whole affair was Sewall's public confession. Stoughton's refusal to repent stands under the proverb, “He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD” (Pro 17:15).
roots_summary: Hebrew ed (H5707), witness; quwm (H6965), to stand, be established; toebah (H8441), abomination.
roots_lines: Hebrew quwm (H6965) — to arise, be established; Deuteronomy 19:15.
usage: “at the mouth of two witnesses” (Deu 19:15) — the law Salem broke.
“he that condemneth the just” (Pro 17:15) — the judgment on the court.
“whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13) — the mercy Sewall sought and Stoughton refused.

pos: n. (Samuel Stone, 1602–1663, teacher of the church at Hartford with Thomas Hooker and co-founder of the town)
etymology: Hebrew Shemuel, heard of God; English Stone, a dweller by a stone.
biblical_def: Samuel Stone was born at Hertford in England, trained at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and silenced for nonconformity before sailing to New England in 1633 on the same ship as Thomas Hooker and John Cotton. He became teacher of the church at Newtown, now Cambridge, Massachusetts, with Hooker as its pastor, and in 1636 the two led most of their congregation through the wilderness to the Connecticut River, where they founded a new town and named it Hartford after Stone's birthplace. Stone served with Hooker until Hooker's death in 1647 and then alone. He was a skilled disputant and a stout defender of the authority of the eldership within the congregational way; his description of a Congregational church as a speaking aristocracy in the face of a silent democracy summed up his conviction that elders rule and the brethren consent. In the 1650s the Hartford church divided bitterly over his authority and over the terms of baptism and membership, and in 1659 a dissenting party withdrew up the river to found Hadley. Stone's doctrine of the eldership rested on the apostolic pattern: “when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23), and on the charge to the flock, “Obey them that have the rule over you” (Heb 13:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an elder as an officer in the church, and a teacher in the New England churches as an officer distinct from the pastor.
webster_full: EL'DER, n. In the primitive church, the elders were persons who enjoyed offices or ecclesiastical functions.
TEACH'ER, n. One who instructs others; in the New England churches, a teaching officer distinguished from the pastor, whose work was chiefly doctrine.
ARIS'TOCRACY, n. A form of government in which the whole supreme power is vested in the principal persons of a state.
scriptures: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
corruption_summary: Hooker's colleague at Hartford, who defended the rule of elders inside the congregational way.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Stone's phrase is often quoted as proof that Puritan churches were undemocratic, as though that were a charge. Scripture's churches were not democracies; they were governed by elders who must give account, and served by a flock that obeyed and consented, as the Jerusalem council's decision “pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church” (Act 15:22).

The honest caveat is the Hartford quarrel itself, in which a teacher's insistence on his authority helped split a church. The principle to recover is Peter's balance: elders rule, but “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3).
roots_summary: Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to ordain; presbuteros (G4245), elder; katakurieuo (G2634), to lord over.
roots_lines: Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to exercise lordship over; 1 Peter 5:3.
usage: “ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the eldership he defended.
“they watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17) — why elders rule.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3) — the limit on their rule.

pos: n. (Nathaniel Morton, 1613–1685, secretary of Plymouth Colony and author of New-Englands Memoriall, 1669)
etymology: Hebrew Nethanel, given of God; English Morton, moor town.
biblical_def: Nathaniel Morton was born at Leiden among the English Separatists of John Robinson's congregation and came to Plymouth in 1623 as a boy; his mother was the sister of Governor William Bradford's wife, and Bradford raised him and trained him in public business. From 1647 until his death he was secretary of Plymouth Colony, keeping its records. In 1669 he published New-Englands Memoriall, the first printed history of the colony, drawn largely from Bradford's unpublished manuscript Of Plymouth Plantation and arranged year by year as a record of God's providences toward the Pilgrims: their exile in Holland, the voyage of the Mayflower, the compact, the first winter's deaths, the friendship of Massasoit, and the deaths of the first generation of leaders. Morton wrote so that the children of New England would remember what God had done for their fathers. Because Bradford's own history was lost for nearly a century, Morton's Memoriall was for generations the chief source of the Pilgrim story. His purpose was the psalmist's: “I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old” (Psa 77:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a memorial as that which preserves the memory of something, and providence as the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
webster_full: MEMO'RIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; any thing that serves to keep in memory.
PROV'IDENCE, n. In theology, the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
SEC'RETARY, n. A person employed by a public body, to write orders, letters, dispatches, public or private papers, records and the like.
scriptures: I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old.
This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
corruption_summary: Plymouth's secretary, who wrote the colony's history as a record of God's providences.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation in reading Morton is to treat his providential history as naive, a pious overlay on events that can be explained without God. Morton wrote as Scripture writes history, as the record of what the LORD has done, and the Psalms command exactly that: “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18).

The principle to recover is that a people that forgets God's dealings with its fathers will soon forget God. Morton's Memoriall is a civic duty performed as worship, written so plainly that, as the prophet says, “he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2).
roots_summary: Hebrew zakar (H2142), to remember; pele (H6382), wonder; kathab (H3789), to write.
roots_lines: Hebrew baar (H874) — to make plain, declare; Habakkuk 2:2.
usage: “I will remember the works of the LORD” (Psa 77:11) — providential history.
“This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) — the purpose of the Memoriall.
“Write the vision, and make it plain” (Hab 2:2) — the secretary's craft.
